paragraphs: Many methods depend on knowing how similar two examples are. Clustering uses similarity to organize data, while individual fairness can use it to express which people should receive comparable treatment. This paper examines a difficult prerequisite: obtaining a reliable similarity function when the examples come from different distributions or demographic groups.

The authors propose a sampling framework that learns similarities across groups with limited expert feedback. Instead of assuming that an accurate comparison rule is already available, their framework makes learning that rule part of the problem. Expert judgments provide information for comparisons that may otherwise be difficult to establish across distinct data sources.

The contribution includes both theoretical bounds and empirical validation across a large collection of experiments. Together, these support the proposed algorithms as an efficient way to learn cross-group similarity. The broader significance is that similarity becomes something to estimate and justify, rather than an unquestioned input to downstream applications such as fairness or clustering.
neurips-2023-comparing-apples-to-oranges.tldr: An efficient sampling framework learns similarity functions across different data distributions using limited expert feedback.

paragraphs: Vision models can become less reliable when their inputs differ from the data encountered during training. Visual prompting adapts the input presented to a model, offering a lightweight way to respond to that shift. However, standard prompts use large additive vectors and rely on labeled data, creating an overfitting problem when adaptation must happen without labels at test time.

This paper introduces convolutional visual prompts, or CVP, for that label-free setting. Their convolutional structure uses fewer than one percent of the trainable parameters required by standard visual prompts. The central idea is to restrict the adaptation through structure, reducing the number of adjustable quantities that could overfit during self-supervised adaptation.

Experiments across varied out-of-distribution visual perception tasks report robustness improvements of up to 5.87 percent over several large-scale models. That figure describes the largest reported improvement, rather than a uniform gain. The findings support structured input adaptation as a practical approach to improving robustness when labels are unavailable at deployment.
neurips-2023-convolutional-visual-prompt.tldr: Convolutional visual prompts use very few trainable parameters to improve vision-model robustness through label-free test-time adaptation.

paragraphs: A classifier that abstains can withhold predictions when it is uncertain. Evaluating only its visible predictions leaves another question unanswered: how well would it have performed if it had been required to predict every time? This matters when withheld predictions might later be used directly or as a fallback.

The paper treats abstentions as missing data and defines a counterfactual score: expected performance without the option to abstain. It gives conditions under which that score can be identified. Stochastic abstentions together with evaluation data independent of training data provide the stated missing-at-random setting. With deterministic abstention, the score is unidentifiable because performance on the withheld cases can be arbitrarily poor.

Under identification, the authors use observational causal-inference tools to develop nonparametric and doubly robust estimators. They examine the approach with simulated and real data. The contribution is a principled way to compare the underlying predictive performance of abstaining systems, with explicit conditions governing when the available observations can support that comparison.
neurips-2023-counterfactually-comparing-.tldr: The paper defines and estimates how abstaining classifiers would perform without abstention, while specifying when that score is identifiable.

paragraphs: Knowledge-graph reasoning faces a tradeoff between explicit rules and learned embeddings. Rules offer precise inferences but are difficult to apply at scale, while embeddings support efficient reasoning with less clear inference accuracy. Combining them requires an approximation that remains useful to both kinds of models without evaluating every possible triple.

DiffLogic addresses this through an adaptive filter that selects essential triples according to the current rules and their weights. It then uses probabilistic soft logic to assess agreement among the selected triples, observed facts, and weighted rules. This formulation accommodates the continuous truth scores produced by embeddings rather than requiring every candidate fact to be simply true or false.

Because this agreement calculation supports differentiable optimization, the framework can alternately update embeddings and weighted rules. Benchmark experiments report improvements over baselines in both effectiveness and efficiency. The approach therefore links its reasoning quality and computational savings to a common design choice: concentrating joint rule-and-embedding optimization on adaptively selected triples.
neurips-2023-differentiable-neuro-symbol.tldr: DiffLogic combines rules and embeddings through adaptive triple selection and differentiable soft logic, improving benchmark effectiveness and efficiency.

paragraphs: Language models can reproduce complete sequences from their training data word for word. This becomes especially concerning when the sequences contain sensitive personal information. Discovering such memorization only after an expensive training run can leave developers with an otherwise useful model that they may need to discard.

The paper investigates whether lower-compute trial runs can predict which sequences a larger model will memorize before its full training is complete. The authors measure memorization across the Pythia model suite and develop scaling relationships for forecasting it. The aim is to use observable behavior from cheaper runs to anticipate memorization in a more costly training setting.

The study also provides recommendations for allocating the same compute budget to improve prediction recall, emphasizing the ability to catch sequences that will be memorized. It reports additional findings about how memorization scores are distributed across models and data, and releases reproducibility materials. These results support early forecasting as a way to assess memorization risk, without claiming that forecasting itself prevents memorization.
neurips-2023-emergent-and-predictable-me.tldr: Measurements from lower-compute Pythia runs support forecasting which training sequences larger language models will memorize.

paragraphs: Generative models that operate on discrete tokens need a way to turn rich signals such as audio into compact representations. The compression step matters because it must reduce the amount of information to model while preserving high-quality sound. This paper develops a neural audio compressor intended to serve that role across different kinds of audio.

The method combines techniques from high-fidelity audio generation with improved vector quantization drawn from image modeling. It also changes the adversarial and reconstruction losses used in training. Together, these choices produce a token representation at 8 kbps for 44.1 kHz audio, corresponding to approximately ninetyfold compression.

A single model handles speech, environmental sounds, music, and other audio domains. Comparisons report significant advantages over competing compression algorithms, and ablation studies examine every design choice. The authors also provide code and trained weights. The stated significance extends beyond compact storage: a universal audio tokenizer can provide a common foundation for generative models covering several forms of sound.
neurips-2023-high-fidelity-audio-compres.tldr: A universal neural audio compressor converts 44.1 kHz audio into high-fidelity tokens at 8 kbps, achieving approximately ninetyfold compression.

paragraphs: Systematic visual imagination means using reusable knowledge to predict what follows from a visual scene, including situations not encountered during training. A model needs both to interpret the image and to apply the world's dynamics to it. This paper introduces the Systematic Visual Imagination Benchmark, or SVIB, to make that ability a direct target of evaluation.

SVIB frames the task as a minimal world-modeling problem: given one image, generate the image produced after one step of underlying dynamics. Its design allows researchers to control how many possible combinations of factors appear during training. This makes it possible to study generalization to new combinations while varying the difficulty of the task.

The benchmark also permits perception and imagination to be optimized together. The authors evaluate a range of baseline models, providing a picture of existing approaches on this problem. Its main contribution is a controlled experimental framework for studying whether visual knowledge can be recombined, rather than a claim that systematic visual imagination has already been solved.
neurips-2023-imagine-the-unseen-world-a-.tldr: SVIB tests whether visual world models can reuse learned knowledge to predict one-step changes for unfamiliar combinations of factors.

paragraphs: Symmetry constraints help neural networks generalize by restricting how their outputs can change when inputs are transformed. Convolutions build such constraints into the architecture, but those choices are fixed in advance. This paper asks whether a network can instead learn how much symmetry to use in each layer directly from data.

The authors address two obstacles: representing flexible layer-level equivariance efficiently, and choosing a learning objective that actually rewards useful constraints. They improve parameterizations of soft equivariance and optimize marginal likelihood using differentiable Laplace approximations. This objective balances agreement with the data against model complexity, giving symmetry a role that a data-fit loss alone does not encourage.

On image classification tasks, the method learns layer-specific equivariances automatically and achieves performance equivalent to or better than baselines with predefined symmetry. The result supports adapting architectural constraints to the task through gradient-based learning. Its significance is the combination of flexible symmetry representations with an objective capable of selecting their strength, rather than requiring every layer's constraints to be prescribed beforehand.
neurips-2023-learning-layer-wise-equivar.tldr: The method learns each layer's symmetry constraints by balancing data fit and model complexity through a differentiable marginal-likelihood objective.

paragraphs: Unsupervised skill discovery aims to learn distinct behaviors, but exploration can stall when skills are heavily penalized for departing from their initial trajectories. Auxiliary rewards based on uncertainty or state entropy have been used to encourage exploration. The authors find that these rewards become less effective as environments grow more complex.

DISCO-DANCE introduces a guided process for reaching new states. It first selects the skill with the greatest potential to access unexplored parts of the environment. Other skills follow this guide, after which they spread out in the newly reached states to become distinguishable from one another. Guidance and diversification therefore serve complementary roles within the discovery process.

The authors evaluate the method on two navigation benchmarks and one continuous-control benchmark, reporting improvements over other unsupervised skill-discovery baselines in challenging environments. These findings support sharing a promising route to unexplored states before encouraging separate behaviors there. The contribution is a concrete exploration strategy that coordinates skills while retaining the objective of learning a diverse repertoire.
neurips-2023-learning-to-discover-skills.tldr: DISCO-DANCE guides skills toward unexplored states with a promising leader, then encourages them to develop distinct behaviors.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems trained on historical behavior have limited access to what a user wants in the current interaction. CORE adds a conversational agent that checks an existing recommender's estimates during an online session. The recommender supplies item relevance scores, and the conversation supplies opportunities to verify them through questions about attributes or individual items.

The framework connects these components through uncertainty minimization. It defines uncertainty as the sum of relevance scores that have not yet been checked, then derives the certainty gained by asking each possible attribute or item question. An online decision-tree algorithm uses these gains to choose what to ask at each turn.

The authors provide a bound on the expected number of conversational turns in a cold-start setting. Experiments show that CORE works with varied recommendation approaches and consistently improves results in both hot-start and cold-start settings. Its significance is a common interface between offline recommendation and online interaction: questions are selected to check estimated relevance rather than requiring a jointly designed reinforcement-learning system.
neurips-2023-lending-interaction-wings-t.tldr: CORE improves recommendations by selecting conversational questions that reduce uncertainty in an existing recommender's relevance estimates.

paragraphs: Medical images differ substantially from the natural images used to train many general-purpose vision models. LVM-Med addresses this mismatch through large-scale self-supervised training on medical data. The authors assemble approximately 1.3 million images from 55 public datasets, covering multiple organs and modalities including CT, MRI, X-ray, and ultrasound.

Alongside benchmarking existing self-supervised algorithms, they introduce a contrastive-learning method based on graph matching. It incorporates prior image similarities using local and global information, and its training objective captures structural relationships among feature embeddings. Gradient-estimation techniques for black-box solvers allow this combinatorial objective to participate in efficient end-to-end training.

Evaluation spans 15 downstream medical tasks, including segmentation, classification, and detection, in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings. The authors report empirical improvements over several supervised, self-supervised, and foundation models. For brain-tumor classification and diabetic-retinopathy grading, they report gains of 6–7 percent over previous vision-language models trained on one billion masks while using a ResNet-50. The findings support medical-domain pretraining combined with structurally informed representation learning.
neurips-2023-lvm-med-learning-large-scal.tldr: LVM-Med combines large-scale medical-image pretraining with graph-based contrastive learning to improve performance across downstream medical tasks.

paragraphs: A generalist web agent needs to follow language instructions across varied websites and interaction patterns. Mind2Web introduces a dataset for developing and evaluating that capability using real websites. It contains more than 2,000 open-ended tasks from 137 websites across 31 domains, paired with crowdsourced sequences of actions.

The dataset addresses the limited diversity and simplified environments of earlier web-agent datasets. The authors also explore language-model-based agents and identify a practical obstacle: real pages often contain too much raw HTML to feed directly into a large language model. Filtering the HTML first with a smaller language model significantly improves both effectiveness and efficiency.

The resulting approach shows a decent level of performance on previously unseen websites and even unseen domains. The authors nevertheless describe substantial remaining room for improvement toward broadly generalizable agents. By releasing the dataset, implementation, and trained models, the work supplies both a testbed and an initial approach for studying instruction-following across realistic web environments.
neurips-2023-mind2web-towards-a-generali.tldr: Mind2Web provides diverse real-website tasks and shows that filtering HTML with a smaller model helps language-model web agents.

paragraphs: Multimodal models combine different kinds of input to make predictions, but parallel fusion can obscure how each input contributes and create dependence on which modalities are available. MultiModN instead combines representations sequentially through a modular pipeline. It accommodates varying numbers, combinations, and types of modalities while supplying detailed predictive feedback for multiple tasks.

This design makes the progression of predictions interpretable and addresses biased missingness. When missing inputs follow systematic patterns, a model can learn those patterns in ways that fail when availability changes at inference. The paper investigates this challenge by simulating missing-not-at-random data and comparing sequential fusion with parallel-fusion baselines.

Across four experiments covering ten tasks in medical diagnosis, academic performance, and weather, sequential fusion does not compromise performance relative to the parallel baseline. Under changed missingness patterns, the parallel baselines suffer catastrophic failures that MultiModN resists. These experiments support the architecture's combination of flexible inputs, granular interpretation, and robustness to the studied biased-missingness shifts.
neurips-2023-multimodnmultimodal-multi-t.tldr: MultiModN sequentially combines modalities to support interpretable multitask prediction and resist the tested changes in biased missingness.

paragraphs: Regret measures how much better a learner could have done by consistently changing its past behavior according to an allowed transformation. Considering more transformations creates a stronger standard of hindsight rationality. In sequential games, the challenge is to strengthen that standard while keeping learning computationally efficient.

The paper proves that any sequential game admits learning with sublinear regret against every linear transformation of the mixed-strategy space, using iterations that take polynomial time in the game-tree size. Sublinear regret means that the regret per iteration vanishes over time. The guarantee concerns linear transformations; it does not assert efficient regret minimization against every possible transformation in sequential games.

This no-linear-swap-regret condition is as strong as no-swap-regret in nonsequential games and stronger than no-trigger-regret in sequential games. The result also establishes a subset of extensive-form correlated equilibria that are robust to linear deviations and can be approached efficiently. It therefore advances both the computational understanding of learning and the strength of equilibrium behavior attainable in sequential interaction.
neurips-2023-polynomial-time-linear-swap.tldr: The paper proves efficient learning with sublinear regret against all linear strategy transformations in any sequential game.

paragraphs: Training a model with differential privacy does not automatically settle the privacy cost of choosing its hyperparameters. Tuning can expose information through the selected values, and evaluating many candidates requires repeated training. Existing private tuning methods that randomize the number of random-search trials can still add substantial privacy and computational costs.

This paper reduces those costs by performing hyperparameter search on a random subset of the sensitive dataset. It then appropriately extrapolates the selected values to the larger dataset. The transfer step is central: tuning uses less data, but its results must remain useful when the final training problem operates at a larger scale.

The authors analyze the proposed method using Rényi differential privacy and experimentally compare it with the earlier randomized-search baseline. They report consistently better privacy–utility tradeoffs in those experiments. The contribution ties together two practical concerns, the privacy bound and the cost of candidate evaluation, through subsampling and the extrapolation of tuning results.
neurips-2023-practical-differentially-pr.tldr: Private hyperparameter tuning on a random data subset, followed by extrapolation, improves the tested privacy–utility tradeoff while targeting lower compute costs.

paragraphs: Time-series diffusion models are often trained for a specific conditional task, such as forecasting. TSDiff explores a more reusable approach: train an unconditional model and introduce task-specific conditioning during inference. Its self-guidance mechanism does this without auxiliary networks or changes to the training procedure.

The paper evaluates three uses of the learned model. For forecasting, TSDiff is competitive with several specialized conditional methods. For refinement, it uses its learned implicit probability density to iteratively improve predictions from base forecasters, with less computational overhead than reverse diffusion. These uses show how the same learned distribution can support both producing predictions and revising existing ones.

TSDiff also generates synthetic training data while retaining its generative performance. Forecasters trained on its samples outperform those trained on samples from other leading time-series generators in the reported experiments, occasionally even exceeding models trained on real data. That occasional result is qualified, while the broader contribution is demonstrating forecasting, refinement, and synthesis from one unconditionally trained model.
neurips-2023-predict-refine-synthesize-s.tldr: TSDiff uses inference-time self-guidance to adapt an unconditional diffusion model for forecasting, prediction refinement, and synthetic time-series generation.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains models without exchanging clients' raw data, but differences between local datasets can reduce the usefulness of a shared model. Personalized federated learning adapts that model to each client. This paper focuses on information specific to clients that the global model may overlook during that process.

The proposed approach injects personalized prior knowledge into the global model at each client. Its pFedBreD framework separates the personalized prior from the local objective, which is regularized using Bregman divergence. This separation is intended to make personalization more adaptable. A relaxed mirror-descent procedure explicitly extracts the prior and offers alternative strategies for using it.

The authors provide a convergence analysis and report state-of-the-art performance on five datasets, with improvements of up to 3.5 percent across eight benchmarks. Additional analyses support the robustness and importance of their design choices. The findings support treating client-specific prior information as an explicit component of personalization, rather than relying solely on local training to recover what the global model overlooks.
neurips-2023-prior-personalized-prior-fo.tldr: pFedBreD injects explicit client-specific priors into federated personalization to recover information that a global model may overlook.

paragraphs: Continual reinforcement learning requires adapting to changing environments while retaining useful behavior from earlier tasks. Inspired by neural rewiring, this paper proposes learning permutations of hidden neurons. The permutation mechanism is trained end to end and can rearrange available synapses, opening up a broad range of weight configurations for adaptation.

Two designs guide the process. A multi-mode rewiring strategy diversifies the policy to encourage exploration in new environments. To preserve earlier behavior, the network caches learned wirings while making subtle weight updates, allowing previous task-appropriate states to be recovered. An alignment mechanism jointly optimizes the cached wirings and weights to balance adaptation with stability.

The method is evaluated in eighteen continual reinforcement-learning scenarios covering locomotion and manipulation. The authors report advantages over leading competitors in the tradeoff between performance and efficiency. The contribution connects exploration and retention through learnable connectivity: new wirings support adaptation, while cached wirings and alignment provide a way to maintain access to earlier task behavior.
neurips-2023-rewiring-neurons-in-non-sta.tldr: Learnable neuron permutations and cached wirings help reinforcement-learning networks adapt to new environments while retaining earlier task behavior.

paragraphs: Transformers are promising substitutes for costly partial-differential-equation simulations, but large spatial grids create computational and numerical difficulties. Even attention mechanisms with linear complexity can remain expensive or unstable at these scales. FactFormer addresses this problem by reorganizing the way a Transformer handles functions defined over multiple spatial dimensions.

A learnable projection decomposes the input function into several sub-functions, each with a one-dimensional domain. These are evaluated to construct an input-dependent kernel through a factorization along the spatial axes. The factorized computation can act as an efficient low-rank substitute for full attention, reducing the burden of handling multidimensional interactions directly.

The authors demonstrate simulations of two-dimensional Kolmogorov flow on a 256-by-256 grid and three-dimensional smoke buoyancy on a 64-by-64-by-64 grid, reporting good accuracy and efficiency. These examples support the proposed factorization as a scalable approach to PDE surrogate modeling. The central contribution is a structured approximation to attention that uses the spatial organization of the problem to make large-grid modeling more practical.
neurips-2023-scalable-transformer-for-pd.tldr: FactFormer factorizes multidimensional attention along spatial axes to support accurate and efficient large-grid PDE surrogate simulations.

paragraphs: A trained perception model can be compared with its reference data through their geometric structure at several scales. This paper introduces topological parallax to make that comparison theoretically and computationally accessible. The authors' proofs and examples show that geometric similarity is essential to trustworthy interpolation and perturbation.

Explicitly describing the geometry of a deep model is typically impossible. Parallax instead uses the reference dataset to examine how geodesic distortions affect a Rips complex. This provides estimates of topological features such as connected components, cycles, and voids, allowing a comparison of the model's structure with the structure represented by the data.

The theoretical formulation uses a bifiltered persistence module, whose key properties remain stable when the reference dataset is perturbed. That stability supports the comparison tool itself. The authors also conjecture that parallax could clarify discussions of overfitting and generalization; this is a proposed implication rather than an established resolution. The contribution is a geometric specification for examining model behavior beyond a single predictive score.
neurips-2023-topological-parallax-a-geom.tldr: Topological parallax compares the multiscale geometry of a trained model and reference data to study trustworthy interpolation and perturbation.

paragraphs: Hierarchical image classification organizes labels into broad ancestor classes and more specific descendants. TransHP uses the broad category as an explicit hint for recognizing the finer category. The motivation is that knowing the general kind of object can help a model focus on subtle distinctions within that group.

The model learns prompt tokens for coarse classes and predicts an image's coarse class at an intermediate Transformer block. It then inserts the corresponding prompt into the intermediate features. Although the model parameters remain the same for every image, this selected token conditions subsequent feature extraction, creating an input-dependent focus within the shared network.

Experiments report improvements in classification accuracy, training-data efficiency, and explainability, as well as favorable comparisons with earlier hierarchical methods. Reported examples include a 2.83 percent ImageNet accuracy improvement for ViT-B/16 and a 12.69 percent improvement when using ten percent of ImageNet training data. These findings support using hierarchy actively during feature extraction, with coarse predictions guiding the discrimination of descendant classes.
neurips-2023-transhp-image-classificatio.tldr: TransHP inserts prompts for predicted coarse classes into a Transformer to guide finer-grained image classification.

paragraphs: Deep equilibrium models and neural ordinary differential equations are implicit neural models developed from different mathematical formulations. This paper connects them through homotopy continuation, a classical approach that solves nonlinear equations using a corresponding differential equation. That connection provides a route for combining properties associated with the two model families.

The resulting model, HomoODE, finds an equilibrium implicitly by solving a modified neural ODE. This replaces the explicit Newton-style equilibrium search described for DEQs with a homotopy-based process. The authors aim to retain the high accuracy of equilibrium models together with the stability of neural ODEs, and accelerate the method using a shared learnable initial point.

The framework also offers an interpretation of augmented neural ODEs when their augmented part is viewed as the equilibrium to be found. Across several image-classification tasks, HomoODE outperforms existing implicit models in accuracy and memory consumption. The contribution is therefore both a mathematical bridge between model families and an experimentally supported architecture derived from that bridge.
neurips-2023-two-sides-of-the-same-coin-.tldr: HomoODE uses homotopy continuation to connect equilibrium models and neural ODEs, improving accuracy and memory use in image-classification experiments.

paragraphs: Bisimulation-based representation learning has shown promise in reinforcement learning, yet its performance can deteriorate when learning only from an offline dataset. This paper investigates that mismatch. Its analysis identifies missing transitions as particularly damaging to estimating bisimulation relationships, helping explain why methods that succeed online may falter offline.

The authors also examine reward scaling, showing its role in bounding both bisimulation measurements and the value errors they induce. They propose two responses: use an expectile operator for representation learning to reduce overfitting to incomplete data, and apply an appropriate reward-scaling strategy to avoid collapse of the learned features.

These changes are implemented in the existing MICo and SimSR algorithms and evaluated on D4RL and Visual D4RL, where they yield performance gains. The findings connect practical improvements to specific weaknesses of offline representation learning. Incomplete transition coverage and reward scale become explicit design concerns, rather than assuming that an online bisimulation method will transfer effectively to a fixed dataset.
neurips-2023-understanding-and-addressin.tldr: Expectile-based representation learning and appropriate reward scaling address incomplete-data overfitting and feature collapse in offline bisimulation methods.

paragraphs: A collection of news videos about one topic can contain material relevant to a larger story. This paper introduces video timeline modeling: creating a timeline associated with that collection to help people understand the story's content and structure. News-story summarization is one potential application of the proposed task.

To support research, the authors build YouTube-News-Timeline, a benchmark containing more than twelve thousand timelines and three hundred thousand YouTube news videos. They also propose quantitative evaluation metrics. The dataset and metrics together establish a common testbed for studying the task and comparing approaches to constructing video-associated timelines.

The authors develop and benchmark several deep-learning approaches using this testbed. The work is presented as an exploratory foundation for further research, with the assets made available to others. Its central contribution is the combination of a new problem formulation, realistic data, evaluation tools, and initial models, giving researchers a concrete basis for investigating how multiple videos can be organized into an understandable news story.
neurips-2023-video-timeline-modeling-for.tldr: The paper introduces video timeline modeling and a large news-video benchmark with evaluation metrics and initial deep-learning approaches.

paragraphs: Flatness regularization favors solutions where the training loss changes less sharply around the learned parameters. Prior work links optimizer randomness to minimizing a sharpness measure, the trace of the loss Hessian, among zero-loss solutions. Although explicit flatness regularization can improve generalization empirically, the reason for that improvement remains unclear.

This paper studies the question in deep matrix factorization, where a deep linear network learns from linear measurements and its overall mapping is the product of its layer matrices. This setting allows the authors to connect a property of the parameter-space loss surface with a property of the matrix represented by the entire network.

Under the Restricted Isometry Property for the measurements, minimizing the Hessian trace is approximately equivalent to minimizing the end-to-end matrix's Schatten 1-norm. The paper connects that preference to better generalization. The result supplies a specific explanation for flatness regularization in this setting, with both the measurement assumption and the approximate nature of the equivalence central to the claim.
neurips-2023-what-is-the-inductive-bias-.tldr: Under a measurement-isometry assumption, Hessian-trace minimization approximately favors low Schatten 1-norm solutions in deep matrix factorization.
